For those unaware the Rooney rule was put in place in 2002 saying that a team can't hire a coach (or other major positions in the organization) until it has interviewed a minority candidate for the job. Wikipedia has a pretty good run down if you want more depth but that's the basic bottom line.

As the coaching carousel begins it's 2016 rotation the Rooney Rule (RR) comes into play again, this time in the form of Sean Payton's future. As this article points out theoretically there are teams that might like to deal for him with the Saints (as I've said before in more depth elsewhere I think all sign point to him staying in NOLA, but since the team has been mum, it's worth discussing), but they can't because if it gets out they want to start talking trade for Payton without having met the RR requirements it would likely lead to minority candidates declining coaching interviews with the team because they would know they have chosen their guy already and the interview would be a patronizing formality (if you're willing to discuss sending picks or cash to get a guy, you're obviously sure he's your guy). And while there's lots of speculation that Payton would only leave NOLA for certain jobs, no one but him knows for sure which ones those are. Heck he might not know. A team that no one would expect he'd go to could make him an offer he couldn't refuse in the form of an insane paycheck, unlimited power, or etc. So you theoretically could have multiple teams with an equal likelihood of landing him. Being the first to get your pitch effort could be the difference in getting him or not. This is especially so in Payton's case of still being under contract with the Saints since any team that wanted him would have to get a deal with both him and the Saints arranged. But theoretically there are teams hamstruck losing valuable time going through the motions of the RR.

First let me address the usual defenses of the RR:

Even if some minorities turn down interviews, there would certainly be someone who would accept the interview even if he thought the job was unlikely to go to him.

Sure. A lower assistant coach, a lower profile college coach, etc might accept an interview for a job they'll never get just for the experience of it or to raise their profile or such. But otherwise "serious" candidates would not, because if you're respected in your own right why would you lower yourself to be someone's box to check off?

It forces teams to go out of their way to look for minority coaches it might otherwise not consider.

I doubt it. Sports has always been at the forefront of equality because at the end of the day sports are a very black and white (no pun intended) results oriented thing. We have the famous instances of Jackie Robinson, Joe Lewis uniting a very racist country against an even more racist country (Schmelling v Lewis), the same racist country rallying around Jessie Owens against the same more racist country, etc. But football has always been even one step ahead of the rest of sports in throwing racial preferences out the window. The NFL desegregated in 1946, ahead of MLB, and it wasn't a national issue the way Robinson's debut was because football fans knew Kenny Washington was an elite college player for white-bread elitist UCLA and could play, and that's all they cared about. Heck, in 1959 Alabama, from ground zero of the civil rights movement and years before with Governor Wallace screamed, "Segregation forever," played an integrated Penn State team in the Liberty Bowl because they wanted to play the best opponent available. Bear Bryant infamously spent the 60s trying to recruit black players (without success because of their, probably justified, fears rather than the football team's efforts). It's ridiculous to think that in the 21st century a multi-billion dollar industry isn't scouring all ranks for the best of the best.

Something has to be done, blacks make up over sixty percent of NFL players but in recent years have averaged only twelve percent of head coaching positions.

Twelve percent is nearly perfectly in line with the percentage of blacks who make up the US population. That's pretty good, especially when you consider that with only 32 jobs to go around one hire is worth more than three percent of the total. As recently as 2011 black HCs made up 25% of the total, nearly twice the proportional general US population. It of course stands out that a so much more significant portion of the player population is black, but I suspect the two trends are unrelated. It is an old trope that "white parents tell their children to study hard to get to college" and "black parents tell their children to excel athletically to get there." But cliches become so for a reason, and for complex socioeconomic reasons (not the least of which many black families still suffer financially because of second, third and etc order effects of segregation) likely couldn't afford to send their children to college (or for those who will make the FAFSA/loan argument don't perceive themselves as being able to afford to because they didn't grow up "in the system" and are unfamiliar). But that doesn't mean white breads don't like football, and a proportional amount of white kids will pursue a career in sports even if they didn't see it as their "way out of the ghetto" and go all in young making it more likely to play college ball and hence be drafted.

Now, back to my original point, that the Rooney Rule isn't just stupid (it makes teams patronize minorities even if it has already selected it's guy), but is bad for minorities. How can a rule that gives minorities more interviews be bad for them? The patronizing. It's easy to see how a rare high profile, coveted coach like Payton on the market could lead to patronizing interviews, but in the background there are no doubt lower profile cases. Let's say a team is interviewing new coach prospects. They interview a guy who happens to be white. He hits it out the park. He pitches everything the team wants to hear, he has amazing rapport with the owner and the front office guys, etc. He's their guy. But the team hasn't met the Rooney Rule requirements. They're going to call in a minority candidate(s) to interview for a job that they will never get. Going back to the idea of getting the coach you want quickly teams around the league will be moving to grab their guy. Going back to the idea of getting the best available teams will be offering deals to the best available. You now have minority coaches who are accepting interviews for jobs they will never get, delaying interviews for jobs they could. You're hurting minorities by sending them on pointless missions. Moreoever MLK's "Judge a man not by the color of his skin but by the merit of his character," comes into play. As previously discussed football is a results oriented thing. And owners and front offices in the 21st century will scour ranks to find winners, because winning is good for business. Being hampered by patronizing is not for anyone. Yet actual racists will cite this line to justify their racism if a RR candidate is hired and fails, as many HCs for a myriad of reasons do, perpetuating racism. Moreover, a post racist society isn't one that goes out of it's way to ignore skin color, but treats it the same as hair or eye color, it is irrelevant.

By all means attack me, agree with me, criticize my position, or defend it. I believe this is a conversation worth having.

When you are cleaning a room, don't try to chew through all the items sequentially. If you try to make a decision with each individual item, you will quickly run out of will power. Additionally, you are making these decisions in the dark since you don't have an idea of the larger picture; e.g., "Do I need this shirt... hm... maybe...?" Whereas if you had first collected all your shirts into a pile, you would see you have 5 green t-shirts already, so maybe you can donate/sell 2-3 of them.

Finally, this has the added benefit of not needing to think during the first phase of cleaning a room. You don't need to get sentimental, tired, or sidetracked - you just pick up each item and think, "Shirt? Pile on bed." "Book? Box on the floor." "Stationary? Pile on desk." "Electronics? Next to stationary." You get the idea!
